bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body: Refinery closure funding was entirely equity-backed (Rs 600cr) rather than debt refinancing, cleaning the balance sheet but diluting equity value temporarily; CPG revenue drop of 48% is a deliberate 'quality over quantity' move to fix unit economics, not demand destruction; Power tariff arbitrage benefits from recent tribunal orders are negligible for EID as they sell primarily via exchanges.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Integrated sugarcane model - sugar, distillery and co-generation off the same cane, giving near-complete cane utilisation and a circular, zero-waste energy loop
- Multi-feed distillery flexibility across molasses, syrup and grain feedstocks, described as an important differentiator in navigating volatile input costs and pricing dynamics
- 'Parry's' brand equity in Southern India, with an estimated ~55% share of the branded sweeteners segment
- Strategic 55.58% equity stake in Coromandel International Limited providing financial flexibility and strategic optionality - demonstrated by funding the PSRIPL closure without undue financial strain
- Membership of the Murugappa Group, cited as a source of financial flexibility and strategic strength
- Karnataka operations as a structural strength - crushing rose to 25.64 LMT with recovery at 12.07% versus 11.74%, against structurally challenged Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh
- Deep farmer-partnership and agri-tech platform - crop development programmes, the 'Cane Insights' control tower, E-Trip Sheet field-to-factory digital tracking and partnerships with Cultyvate, Jiva and Boomitra securing cane supply
- Short-term credit rating maintained at A1+ for the commercial paper programme, underscoring liquidity strength
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Sugarcane availability — structural decline in cane acreage, especially in Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh — Adverse weather, water scarcity, pest and disease outbreaks and farmers shifting to more remunerative alternative crops may reduce cane availability and hit profitability. The Company has already discontinued operations at Pettavathalai, Pudukkottai and Puducherry; existing units at Nellikuppam, Pugalur, Sivagangai and Sankili remain significantly impacted by declining cane/molasses availability and, if the trend persists, their long-term financial viability may be affected. Management concedes that farmer-engagement, Clean Seed Programme, seaweed-based solutions, mechanised harvesting and R&D initiatives may not fully mitigate the structural risk in these two States.
- Raw material pricing — cane price is administered and decoupled from sugar prices — Sugarcane prices are determined by the Central and State Governments and are not directly aligned with prevailing sugar prices; any mismatch resulting in unviable cane pricing directly compresses Sugar Division profitability. Mitigation is limited to advocacy through ISMA and SISMA.
- Sugar price risk — FRP rises without a corresponding MSP revision — Any increase in the Fair and Remunerative Price for sugarcane without a matching increase in the Minimum Support Price for sugar adversely impacts profitability. The Company offsets partially by shifting sales to institutional and retail segments that command a premium over the trade channel and by pushing value-added products such as Amrit and jaggery.
- Water availability and management — Failure or inadequacy of monsoons, depletion of groundwater levels and deterioration in groundwater quality threaten a water-intensive crop. The Company has adopted advanced water treatment technologies (MWTS, JIVA Water Device) and commenced sensor-based autonomous irrigation to cut consumption and lift productivity.
- Shortage of harvesting labour — Non-availability of migrant labour for cane harvesting can delay timely harvesting and hurt overall productivity and recovery. Mitigation relies on local labour, self-harvesting by farmers, mechanised harvesting and wider row planting to enable machine use.
- Regulatory and policy risk in a cyclical industry — Business economics of the integrated sugar industry are significantly influenced by laws and Government policies governing sugarcane and sugar availability, pricing, power tariffs, molasses availability, and ethanol production and sales; stoppage of production due to non-compliance with pollution control regulations, labour laws or other statutory requirements is a further exposure. Financial implication is flagged as negative. Mitigation is the integrated model (sugar + distillery + bagasse-based green energy), value-added products from by-products, business continuity planning, and engagement with Government through industry bodies.
- Employee health and safety — Unsafe practices and an inadequate work environment may create safety risks affecting employee well-being. Mitigation includes behavioural safety capability-building at all levels, a defined maturity roadmap, and a benchmarked Safety Drive with an Action Tracking System, incident reporting, inspections and structured safety observation processes.
- Cyber security and IT system availability — System unavailability or failure of critical IT systems could disrupt business operations, arising from inadequate processes, cyber security vulnerabilities or insufficient backup and disaster recovery. Mitigation includes reviewed backup and disaster recovery policies, firewalls and SIEM monitoring, and periodic user training and awareness.

business.body: The Company crushes sugarcane at six sugar plants across Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh and converts the cane almost fully: sucrose into sugar, molasses/syrup and grain into ethanol and Extra Neutral Alcohol at five distilleries, and bagasse into steam and power used captively and exported to the grid. It sells sugar through institutional and premium channels and markets branded sweeteners (brown sugar, jaggery, low-GI sugar and other premium variants) and staples (rice, pulses, millets) under the 'Parry's' franchise across Southern India, while ethanol is supplied to oil marketing companies under the national blending programme. A nutraceuticals business, including wholly owned US Nutraceuticals Inc., makes organic spirulina, chlorella, carotenoids, astaxanthin and lutein/zeaxanthin largely for export markets.

outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Disciplined Renewal — transform the company into a more focused food, nutrition and bioenergy enterprise, prioritising strengthening of existing operations and extracting greater value from past investments over accelerating expansion
- Prune the portfolio to preserve balance sheet strength: exit from the Parry Sugars refinery business after assessing its operational challenges, structural viability and capital intensity, and redeploy capital towards businesses with stronger long-term relevance and return potential
- Project Propel — a targeted initiative to improve cost efficiency and execution discipline across commercial and manufacturing operations in Sugar and Biofuel
- Strengthen the core across business verticals in FY 2026-27 with focus on margin improvement through sharper cost, portfolio and channel strategies, alongside stronger working capital and cash flow management
- Accelerate digital and AI-led transformation across agriculture, manufacturing and enterprise functions to improve decision-making, productivity and execution discipline
- Build out value-added sweeteners: strengthen the premium 'browns' portfolio (jaggery and differentiated sweetening products) to increase the overall profit pool, including expansion of the Karnataka jaggery facility and a second jaggery unit at Bagalkot
- Recalibrate the Consumer Products Group towards revenue quality, profitability and disciplined capital allocation — repositioning both sweeteners and staples on a more capital-efficient, profitability-led distribution model, with staples managed selectively for cash efficiency rather than broad-based expansion
- Remain open to selective inorganic portfolio expansion in adjacent food categories such as culinary products, spices, ethnic snacks and dessert mixes where strategically relevant and commercially attractive
- Enhance value realisation from by-products, particularly bagasse, through sustainable packaging, soilless media and other value-added applications
- In Nutraceuticals, rebuild momentum in European and U.S. markets, strengthen a science-led differentiated portfolio, expand private label offerings for leading global brands, scale presence in plant-based green blends, and enter new segments such as derma and hair health
- Farmer-first operating model — timely payments, sustained agroeconomic support and continuous field engagement — as the base for cane availability and operational resilience
- Embed sustainability as a strategic enabler: water stewardship, resource efficiency, renewable energy and circular practices at farm and operational level
- Engage with Government and industry bodies (ISMA) for a revision in sugar MSP and rationalisation of ethanol procurement prices
- Governance is anchored in the Murugappa Group ethos and the Five Lights values (Integrity, Passion, Quality, Respect and Responsibility), with the Board exercising oversight over significant strategic, financial, operational and compliance matters through at least quarterly meetings and a maximum gap between meetings of 120 days. Pursuant to Regulation 43A of the Listing Regulations, the Company has a Board-approved Dividend Distribution Policy published on its website. Capital deployment intent during the year was defensive and portfolio-cleansing rather than expansionary: the Company supported its wholly owned refinery subsidiary PSRIPL through rights-issue equity infusions during the year and after the year end specifically to enable it to meet closure-related obligations, having concluded that closure of the loss-making refinery was in the best long-term interest of the Company and its stakeholders. ESG capital and disclosure discipline is reflected in BRSR reporting against the nine NGRBC principles with independent assurance obtained on the BRSR Core indicators. Governance hygiene includes annual board, committee and individual director evaluation, an independent directors' meeting held without management, and no equity or convertible securities held by any Non-Executive Director as on March 31, 2026.
- Safety maturity target: a defined roadmap has been established to enable all locations to achieve 'Established' safety maturity levels by FY 2026-27
- Water stewardship: commenced implementation of sensor-based autonomous irrigation systems designed to operate with minimal or no manual intervention to optimise water-use efficiency and enhance sugarcane productivity, alongside advanced water treatment technologies (MWTS and the JIVA Water Device) to improve water vitality and soil health
- Green energy and circularity: integrated business model with cogeneration using bagasse as fuel, plus development of value-added products from sugar and its by-products to enhance resource efficiency and diversify revenue
- BRSR disclosure and assurance: ESG disclosures made against the nine NGRBC principles on a standalone reporting boundary, with limited assurance on BRSR Core indicators obtained from Price Waterhouse Chartered Accountants India LLP
- Board gender diversity: women constitute 22.22% of the Board of Directors
- Grievance redressal mechanisms are in place for every stakeholder group (communities, shareholders, investors, employees and workers, customers, value chain partners), with 4 shareholder complaints pending at year end subsequently resolved at the beginning of FY 2026-27
- Materiality approach: sustainability issues are classified as material on two criteria — principal risk to operations and financial performance, and relevance to stakeholders — with the assessment linked to the Risk Management section of the Board's Report
- CSR under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 was not applicable to the Company for FY 2025-26
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: FY 2025-26 was a consolidation year rather than an expansion year: capital expenditure remained largely moderate and was directed towards routine modernisation and operational efficiency improvements. The main capacity story is the distillery platform, with FY 2025-26 being the second full year of operations at the expanded capacity of 582 KLPD — comprising the 120 KLPD facility at Haliyal, the 45 KLPD expansion at Nellikuppam commissioned in FY 2024-25, and the 120 KLPD multi-feed grain-based facility at Sankili, Andhra Pradesh. The Sankili grain facility operated below optimal utilisation during the year and is still stabilising. Multi-feed capability across Sankili, together with molasses and syrup-based operations at Haliyal, Nellikuppam, Sivagangai and Bagalkot, allows feedstock optimisation as market and policy conditions evolve. In the Consumer Products Group, the Company commissioned its own dal processing facility during the year, strengthening backward integration and enhancing quality control, and expanded its distribution footprint across modern trade, e-commerce platforms and rural and semi-urban markets. The Company is also evaluating expansion of its consumer portfolio through strengthened R&D capabilities and a mix of organic and inorganic growth initiatives. On the divestment side, operations of the wholly owned sugar refinery subsidiary Parry Sugars Refinery India Private Limited (PSRIPL) — an SEZ-based export-oriented refinery unit at Vakalapudi Village, Kakinada — ceased with effect from the close of working hours on March 31, 2026. PSRIPL must now obtain regulatory approvals including from the Development Commissioner, Vishakapatnam Special Economic Zone and the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, complete the SEZ exit process, then dismantle and dispose of the entire assets of the Refinery Unit, possibly in one or more tranches depending on commercial feasibility, and surrender the leased land to the lessor. The transaction is at a preliminary stage: purchaser identity, timeline and consideration cannot be determined yet, and disposal is intended to proceed through a competitive bidding / open tender process with proceeds applied to PSRIPL's outstanding liabilities. Shareholder approval for the disposal was sought as a Special Resolution at the Fifty First AGM scheduled for August 12, 2026. Looking forward, management expects capital expenditure to remain controlled, with incremental working capital requirements rather than capex keeping debt levels relatively elevated.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Karnataka operations are expected to provide greater stability to the overall sugar business, supported by improved cane availability and favourable climatic conditions
- Cane availability in Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh remains a structural challenge from water scarcity, adverse weather, higher cost of cultivation and farmers shifting to alternative crops — expected to continue exerting pressure on those regions
- A revision in the MSP for sugar and an upward adjustment in ethanol procurement prices remain critical to industry profitability; any favourable revision would significantly enhance the earnings potential of both the sugar and distillery segments
- The cost optimisation programme continued during FY 2025-26 and has resulted in significant rationalisation across the manufacturing value chain; benefits are expected to be sustained going forward
- Foray into jaggery is being expanded to capitalise on increasing consumer preference for brown and natural sweeteners as alternatives to refined sugar
- CPG is expected to enter FY 2026-27 on a stronger operational footing after channel correction and receivables clean-up, with tighter credit discipline and strengthened collections improving working capital efficiency
- Corrective and strategic CPG measures taken in FY 2025-26 are expected to translate into improved operational and financial performance from FY 2026-27 onwards
- Financial flexibility from the strategic stake in Coromandel International Limited and the institutional strength of the Murugappa Group supports the transition into a diversified food, nutrition and biofuel enterprise without compromising the credit profile
- Global dietary supplements market is projected to grow at a CAGR of approximately 7% between 2025 and 2030 to around USD 64 billion, with key markets in the United States, China and Western Europe and emerging opportunity in Asia-Pacific, the Middle East and Africa
- Nutraceutical demand themes: gut health, longevity and healthy ageing, vitality, mental well-being, sleep quality, weight management including the impact of GLP-1 therapies, and women's health; green blends are a strategically important category to scale
- Continued growth is expected in the joint health and Astaxanthin segments, projected to outperform other nutraceutical categories in the coming years
- Nutraceuticals margin risk from intense price competition from imports — over 75% of Asian Spirulina products are sourced from China at lower prices — plus US tariffs and geopolitical uncertainty
- Premium positioning in certified organic Spirulina (estimated 17-20% share of the certified organic segment versus roughly 4% of the global Spirulina market by volume) supports differentiation against low-cost alternatives
- Sugar and Distillery together contributed approximately 77% of revenues, Consumer Products around 20%, with Co-generation and Nutraceuticals smaller but strategically important
- Ethanol demand mix shifted in favour of grain-based ethanol while cane ethanol pricing had yet to reflect the evolving demand landscape; industry-wide capacity additions moderated near-term economics for sugar-based ethanol producers
- Rising need for calibrated brand-building, advertising and promotional expenditure in consumer categories could pressure margins during portfolio transition or channel restructuring
outlook.title: Demand & outlook drivers

deepdive.thesis: EID Parry executed a strategic exit from the loss-making refinery business (infusing ~Rs 600cr to clear debts) while pivoting CPG towards high-margin sweeteners to fix profitability, though Q4 PAT was severely impacted by refinery closure costs despite operational stability in sugar and ethanol segments.

open.item: Shareholder approval was sought at the AGM on August 12, 2026 under Regulation 24(6) of the Listing Regulations for the Board to sell, dispose or lease assets of material subsidiary PSRIPL where the aggregate value in a financial year may exceed twenty percent of PSRIPL's total assets.
Certain units in Tamil Nadu are expected to continue operations during the special crushing season in June-July 2026, supported by favourable late-season cane availability.
The transitional costs from the Consumer Products Group channel correction exercise are expected to normalise from FY 2026-27 onwards.

With structural improvements embedded in the operating model, the Company expects revenues to grow in a stable and sustained manner from FY 2026-27 onwards, supported by steady distillery volumes, improving realisations and a recalibrated, more efficient CPG platform.
The Company expects the corrective and strategic measures undertaken during FY 2025-26 to translate into improved operational and financial performance for the CPG business from FY 2026-27 onwards.
Accelerating digital and AI-led transformation will remain an important focus area in FY 2026-27, enabling better decision-making, enhanced productivity and greater execution discipline.

For FY 2026-27 the Company will continue strengthening the core across business verticals while focusing on margin improvement through sharper cost, portfolio and channel strategies, alongside stronger working capital and cash flow management.

Operating focus to remain centred on the five core businesses - sugar, distillery, co-generation, nutraceuticals and consumer products - supported by the strategic shareholding in Coromandel International Limited.
The nutraceuticals business progressed entry into new segments such as derma and hair health, supported by leadership and organisational restructuring at the U.S. subsidiary Valensa International.
The Company is evaluating opportunities to expand its consumer portfolio through strengthened R&D capabilities and a mix of organic and inorganic growth initiatives.

Capital expenditure is expected to remain controlled, but incremental working capital requirements are likely to keep debt levels relatively elevated, with improvement in leverage metrics over the medium term dependent on sustained cash generation and prudent capital deployment.

Following the closure of PSRIPL's refinery unit, the Company will complete the SEZ exit and dismantle and dispose of the entire assets of the Refinery Unit, potentially in one or more tranches, through a competitive bidding / open tender process, and surrender the leased land to the lessor.
The grain-based Sankili facility operated below optimal utilisation levels during the year and is still gradually stabilising.

Management flags that without supportive policy interventions and incentives for cane cultivation to arrest the decline in acreage in Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh, certain units could face risks to their economic viability.

Disciplined capital deployment remains a central priority — emphasis on improving asset utilisation, strengthening working capital efficiency and enhancing cash generation rather than accelerating expansion.

The Company's key strategic objective is to strengthen its leadership position in the dietary supplements and functional food markets in the United States and Europe, where it holds an estimated 17-20% share of the certified organic Spirulina segment against roughly 4% of the global Spirulina market by volume.

In nutraceuticals the Company will strengthen scientifically validated products, expand private label offerings for leading global brands, enhance presence in plant-based green blends and explore new markets including Canada, the Middle East, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Africa.

Board focus on strengthening the integrated sugarcane value chain, scaling the Consumer Products Group into a meaningful consumer platform, and enhancing the cane supply base through continued investments in precision agriculture and farmer engagement.
The Company is exploring opportunities to enhance value realisation from by-products, particularly bagasse, through sustainable packaging, soilless media and other value-added applications.
The Company remains open to portfolio expansion through selective inorganic opportunities in adjacent food categories such as culinary products, spices, ethnic snacks and dessert mixes.

risks.note: Adverse weather, water scarcity, pest and disease outbreaks and farmers shifting to more remunerative alternative crops may reduce cane availability and hit profitability. The Company has already discontinued operations at Pettavathalai, Pudukkottai and Puducherry; existing units at Nellikuppam, Pugalur, Sivagangai and Sankili remain significantly impacted by declining cane/molasses availability and, if the trend persists, their long-term financial viability may be affected. Management concedes that farmer-engagement, Clean Seed Programme, seaweed-based solutions, mechanised harvesting and R&D initiatives may not fully mitigate the structural risk in these two States.
risks.risk: Sugarcane availability — structural decline in cane acreage, especially in Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh

risks.note: Sugarcane prices are determined by the Central and State Governments and are not directly aligned with prevailing sugar prices; any mismatch resulting in unviable cane pricing directly compresses Sugar Division profitability. Mitigation is limited to advocacy through ISMA and SISMA.
risks.risk: Raw material pricing — cane price is administered and decoupled from sugar prices

risks.note: Any increase in the Fair and Remunerative Price for sugarcane without a matching increase in the Minimum Support Price for sugar adversely impacts profitability. The Company offsets partially by shifting sales to institutional and retail segments that command a premium over the trade channel and by pushing value-added products such as Amrit and jaggery.
risks.risk: Sugar price risk — FRP rises without a corresponding MSP revision

risks.note: Failure or inadequacy of monsoons, depletion of groundwater levels and deterioration in groundwater quality threaten a water-intensive crop. The Company has adopted advanced water treatment technologies (MWTS, JIVA Water Device) and commenced sensor-based autonomous irrigation to cut consumption and lift productivity.

Non-availability of migrant labour for cane harvesting can delay timely harvesting and hurt overall productivity and recovery. Mitigation relies on local labour, self-harvesting by farmers, mechanised harvesting and wider row planting to enable machine use.

Business economics of the integrated sugar industry are significantly influenced by laws and Government policies governing sugarcane and sugar availability, pricing, power tariffs, molasses availability, and ethanol production and sales; stoppage of production due to non-compliance with pollution control regulations, labour laws or other statutory requirements is a further exposure. Financial implication is flagged as negative. Mitigation is the integrated model (sugar + distillery + bagasse-based green energy), value-added products from by-products, business continuity planning, and engagement with Government through industry bodies.
risks.risk: Regulatory and policy risk in a cyclical industry

risks.note: Unsafe practices and an inadequate work environment may create safety risks affecting employee well-being. Mitigation includes behavioural safety capability-building at all levels, a defined maturity roadmap, and a benchmarked Safety Drive with an Action Tracking System, incident reporting, inspections and structured safety observation processes.

System unavailability or failure of critical IT systems could disrupt business operations, arising from inadequate processes, cyber security vulnerabilities or insufficient backup and disaster recovery. Mitigation includes reviewed backup and disaster recovery policies, firewalls and SIEM monitoring, and periodic user training and awareness.
risks.risk: Cyber security and IT system availability
